Issued at 616 PM EDT Wed Oct 14 2026

When the long term forecast period opens on Friday morning, Eastern 
Kentucky will be on the precipice of a significant change in 
airmass. A robust, positively-tilted trough stretching from the 
Central Plains to the Upper Midwest will dig deeper into the Ohio 
and Tennessee River Valleys as the day progresses. At the surface, 
this translates to a deepening cyclone over the eastern Great Lakes 
and a sharp cold front trailing behind it. That cold front will be 
the focal point of Friday's forecast, with sensible weather details 
such as high temperatures and wind direction dependent upon a given 
place's position relative to the boundary.

The entire CWA will experience mild AM lows in the upper 60s on 
Friday morning, when forecast guidance collectively resolves the 
boundary off to the west in the Bluegrass. Pre-frontal surface winds 
will be out of the southwest. So will the flow aloft, and this 
vertical continuity suggests that there will be warm air advection 
ongoing on Friday in places out ahead of the front. FROPA has 
trended a little bit later in the day, and Friday's forecast highs 
have accordingly risen a few degrees towards the upper 70s in our 
easternmost counties. In counties further to the north and west, 
there will be a shorter window of time where this WAA overlaps with 
the diurnal warming cycle. So, high temperatures in places like the 
Bluegrass will only be a few degrees warmer than those lows (in the 
upper 60s/lower 70s). Those highs will also likely occur much 
earlier in the day than usual, as once FROPA occurs, diurnal heating 
will become suppressed by cloud cover and a sharp wind shift. 

Surface winds should shift towards a westerly and then northwesterly 
orientation as FROPA occurs from west to east on Friday. Frontal and 
orographic lift will combine to yield additional light rain shower 
chances along and behind the boundary, but the bigger story with 
this boundary will be the robust cold air advection that takes place 
behind it. Given the tightening pressure gradient of the parent 
synoptic system, Friday afternoon's post-frontal winds will be quite 
breezy. The REFS high-resolution ensemble resolves a 50-80% chance 
of wind gusts in excess of 25 mph across most of the JKL CWA in this 
time frame. When this criteria is lowered to >20 mph, the 
probabilities jump to near 100%. If it is raised above 30 mph, the 
odds dwindle off significantly. While wind advisory criteria is 
unlikely to be met, the magnitude of these winds reinforces the 
notion that there will be an efficient cold air advection regime in 
the wake of Friday afternoon's frontal passage. Expect a significant 
drop in temperatures to occur on Friday evening, with temperatures 
in the 50s area-wide by sunset. Once the sun goes down and solar 
insolation goes away, the temperature plummet will continue. The 
entire CWA should wake up to temperatures in the 40s on Saturday 
morning, but lingering cloud cover and some upsloped rain showers 
should prevent it from getting much colder than that. 

The same cannot be said for Saturday night/Sunday morning, which 
looks to be the coldest night of the autumn season thus far. As a 
post-frontal surface high pressure system builds into the CWA on 
Saturday morning, winds will shift to a more northerly orientation. 
This will bring an end to any orographically-enhanced post-frontal 
rain chances, and a much cooler/drier continental airmass will move 
into the region in the wake of the precipitation. Highs will 
struggle to get much warmer than the 50s, and dewpoints will plummet 
into the 30s on Saturday afternoon. Diurnal mixing should work to 
erode any lingering cloud cover by sunset, which should set the 
stage for efficient radiational cooling overnight. NBM ensemble data 
resolves a 60-90% chance of temperatures dropping below 36 degrees 
across most of the JKL CWA overnight. The most sheltered and shaded 
valleys could make a run at the 32 degree mark, but the probability 
of occurrence drops to below 40% at this threshold. As a reminder, 
the criteria for a Frost Advisory is defined as minimum shelter 
forecast temperatures between 33 and 36 degrees Fahrenheit during 
the growing season, on nights with good radiational cooling 
conditions. Saturday night is poised to meet this criteria, so 
agricultural interests and recreational gardeners are encouraged to 
monitor for potential product issuances as the time approaches.  
  
Temperatures will be slow to make a full recovery back above the 70 
degree mark next week, although a gradual warm-up is expected. The 
postfrontal high should shift east on Sunday as the mid/upper level 
trough axis aloft swings through New England. Antecedent forecast 
thinking is that a building ridge will allow temperatures to 
moderate back into the 60s under fair skies by early next week.
